issues.description: The UML diagram in the problem statement defines the class as 'Course' while the textual description and the template/solution use the class name 'Lecture'. This naming inconsistency in the problem statement can confuse students about what class they are expected to implement and where to place the attributes and methods.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the problem statement consistent by renaming the UML class from 'Course' to 'Lecture' (or update the textual description to refer to 'Course' everywhere). Ensure the UML attributes and methods refer to 'Lecture' so students clearly know which class to implement.

issues.description: The problem text and template/solution refer to a Lecture class, but the UML diagram in the problem statement names the class Course. This mismatch between 'Lecture' and 'Course' can confuse students when mapping the UML to the template code and implementation, making it unclear which class they should implement.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the class name consistent across artifacts. Change the UML diagram's class name from 'Course' to 'Lecture' (or, if 'Course' was intended, rename the template and solution class and references to 'Course') so that the textual description, UML, template, and solution all use the same identifier.
